newsitem.title: MEXICO: Zedillo jeered in Mexico May Day celebration.
newsitem.headline: Zedillo jeered in Mexico May Day celebration.

text.p: Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo was met by jeers and whistles of protest on Thursday, upsetting a carefully staged pro-government May Day rally before the country's most powerful labor confederation.

The whistles, a sort of Mexican catcall, came from a crowd of 10,000 people selected from the six-million strong Confederation of Mexican Workers (CTM), a top labor group long allied with the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).
"Brother Zedillo, help my pocketbook," some of the workers chanted during Zedillo's speech at the National Auditorium.

The address got off to a bad start when Victor Flores, a top labor leader and event organizer, introduced him as "President of the United States," leaving off an important word in the official name of the United Mexican States.
Workers erupted into a chorus of boos and shouts of "Mexico! Mexico!"

Making matters worse for Zedillo, Fidel Velazquez, 97, the ailing CTM chief and a key government ally, failed to turn up on stage with the president due to illness. It was the veteran labor leader's first missed May Day in six decades.
Later on Thursday, independent and radical left unions marched toward the city center, spewing a trail of litter and graffiti in separate rowdy anti-government protests.
Crowds flooded the Mexico City's central plaza with chants such as, "Listen Zedillo, the workers are screwed," and others asking for higher wages or criticizing the PRI.
The unions claimed up to 500,000 people participated in the marches, many obligated to attend by their organizations. More conservative estimates were as low as 50,000.

Velazquez, a former dairy worker and founder of the CTM, has been a traditional supporter of the PRI and is said to have kept Mexican labor unrest under wraps even as wages took a blow following the recession caused by the sudden December 1994 peso devaluation.
Although labor officials have said Velazquez will lead the CTM until his death, many have begun to look for possible successors.
Velazquez' current stand-in, electrician union leader Leonardo Rodriguez was rudely heckled and interruped during his speech before the CTM faithful earlier in the day.

Despite the scattering of jeers, most of the CTM workers showed enthusiasm for Zedillo, giving him hearty rounds of applause and waving pro-governent banners in a sign that, though weakened, the traditional government-labor marriage remains intact.
